analysis.one_liner: Bans surprise out-of-network medical bills for people in employer self-insured health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or vote and died at the end of the 116th Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the federal employee-benefits law so that people covered by self-insured employer health plans could not be billed for the unpaid balance when they get emergency care or are treated at an in-network facility by a doctor who is not in their network. Insurers' plans would have to charge patients only their normal in-network copays and deductibles, and disputes between employers and providers would go to voluntary binding arbitration. The bill was never taken up by the committee it was assigned to and expired when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families in self-insured employer health plans — roughly the majority of people with employer coverage — who today can receive a second bill from an out-of-network emergency room doctor or anesthesiologist after seeking in-network or emergency care. They would owe only their normal in-network cost-sharing, and no prior authorization could be required for ambulance transport or treatment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with employer self-insured health plans

how_it_helps.text: Emergency services providers would be barred from billing a self-insured plan member for any amount beyond the plan's normal copay, coinsurance, or deductible, and the plan must pay the provider directly [S2][S3].

If out-of-network care is used, cost sharing — including the deductible and out-of-pocket limit — must be the same as if the provider were in-network, and prior authorization cannot be required for pre-hospital transport or treatment [S3].

Facility-based providers (such as anesthesiologists or radiologists working at a hospital) could not balance bill a patient for non-emergency services at an in-network facility when the patient had no chance to pick an in-network provider [S2][S3].

Disputes over out-of-network payments would be resolved by the provider's claim amount, the usual and customary community rate, an agreed amount, or voluntary binding arbitration run by neutral organizations with conflict-of-interest rules [S2][S3].
Plans would have to publish monthly-updated provider directories and warn members annually about the possibility of balance billing with out-of-network providers [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Self-insured employers, whose plans would be solely liable for paying out-of-network emergency and facility-based providers, potentially at the provider's claimed charge or the community's usual rate. Out-of-network emergency and facility-based providers would lose the ability to collect balances directly from patients.

drawbacks.text: The default payment options include simply paying 'the amount of the claim made by the provider,' which gives providers little reason to moderate their first invoice and could raise what employers pay [S3].
The protections apply only to self-insured group health plans; people with fully-insured plans or no coverage at all would not benefit, leaving much of the surprise-billing problem untouched [S2].

The arbitration rule that a non-prevailing party pays review costs, judged against settlement offers, rewards aggressive initial offers and could favor whichever side — typically a large employer plan or a provider group — can better afford the process [S3].
Arbitration eligibility thresholds ($3,000 for facility claims, $500 for professional claims) leave smaller disputed bills without a formal resolution route [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient protections are real and target the classic surprise-billing scenarios — emergency care and unavoidable out-of-network providers at in-network hospitals. The weaknesses are in the payment side: defaults that lean toward paying the provider's claimed amount could raise employer costs, and the bill covers only self-insured plans, so a large share of the insured population is left out. A narrower but better-drafted fix covering all plan types with a benchmark-based payment standard would have protected more people at more predictable cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in August 2019, but the committee never scheduled it for a hearing or vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Ross Spano introduced the bill on August 30, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor at any point during the bill's life [S4].
The only recorded activity after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks in the House on September 10, 2019 [S5].
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no action in the Senate, and expired with the Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Out-of-network emergency and facility-based providers keep the ability to bill patients directly for unpaid balances, and self-insured employers avoid new payment obligations. Patients with surprise bills are no better off from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Ross Spano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Bobby Scott (D-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in August 2019 and never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan pattern of support or opposition ever formed in the record.

industries.industry: Out-of-network emergency and facility-based providers (ER physicians, anesthesiologists, radiologists, hospitals)
industries.note: These providers earn revenue by billing patients directly for the gap between their charges and what an insurer pays. The bill would cut off that revenue stream for self-insured plan patients, which is why provider groups fought similar proposals. Patients would stop receiving surprise second bills.

Their plans would become solely liable for out-of-network emergency and facility-based claims, potentially paying the provider's claimed charge or the community's usual rate. Employers bear the cost of protecting their employees, but also gain from workers no longer facing ruinous surprise bills.

The bill would create a new stream of government contracts for neutral arbitration organizations handling billing disputes between plans and providers, with conflict-of-interest rules excluding firms recently tied to health plans or providers.
